stem:
A 27-year-old woman in the emergency department has fever, neck stiffness and photophobia. She is alert, orientated and asking sensible questions. The registrar plans an urgent diagnostic lumbar puncture, and a junior doctor is asked to prepare her.

What must happen before the needle is inserted?

options.A: Proceed on implied consent because suspected meningitis is an emergency
options.B: Have her partner sign the consent form because she is feeling so unwell
options.C: Explain its purpose, what it involves, its risks and alternatives, then get her consent
options.D: Describe the steps of the procedure but leave out the risks so that she does not become distressed
options.E: Carry out the procedure now and talk it through with her once she feels better

correct_answer: C. Explain its purpose, what it involves, its risks and alternatives, then get her consent
why_correct: She is alert and orientated, so she is presumed to have capacity and her own valid consent is needed before an invasive procedure. Valid consent means she has been told the reason for the test, what it involves, the material risks such as post-procedure headache, bleeding and infection, and the reasonable alternatives. The urgency of possible meningitis does not remove the need for consent when the patient can give it. Source: Decision making and consent, GMC, 2020.
why_wrong: A. Implied consent is not enough for an invasive procedure in a patient who can be asked directly. B. Another adult cannot consent on behalf of an adult who has capacity. D. Leaving out material risks makes consent invalid. E. Consent must be obtained before, not after, the procedure.
pearl: In suspected bacterial meningitis, lumbar puncture is done before antibiotics only if it is safe and will not cause a clinically significant delay, so the consent discussion should be prompt and focused.
thinking: Alert, orientated adult ↓ Capacity is presumed ↓ Invasive procedure needs valid consent ↓ Valid consent needs reason, procedure, material risks and alternatives ↓ Explain fully and obtain her agreement beforehand
exam_trap: A, Implied consent because it is an emergency — urgency feels like a reason to skip the discussion, but the emergency exception applies only when consent cannot be obtained, and she is able to give it.
takeaway: A patient who has capacity must give informed consent before an invasive procedure, even when the clinical situation is urgent.
notes: Checker: Stem implied routine imaging before LP; NICE NG240 does LP before antibiotics only if safe and without clinically significant delay, CT only when indicated - stem reworded and pearl corrected to match. Key was longest (shortened; D and B lengthened). Source added. Overlap noted (not dropped): live BX010 and u74-g03 PAN1519/PAN724 test consent content, but none in an urgent setting where 'emergency = implied consent' is the trap - clinician to confirm.

stem:
A 76-year-old woman with delirium on an orthopaedic ward is told about a proposed hip operation. She explains it back accurately straight away, but within a few minutes has no memory of the conversation and cannot hold the details in mind long enough to reach a decision.

Which part of the capacity test is she failing?
why_correct: The Mental Capacity Act functional test requires a person to understand, retain, use or weigh information, and communicate a decision. She understands it at first but cannot keep it in mind long enough to decide, so retention is impaired. Information only needs to be retained long enough to make the decision, so short retention may still be enough if it allows that. Source: Mental Capacity Act 2005 section 3, UK Parliament, 2005; Decision-making and mental capacity (NG108), NICE, 2018.
why_wrong: B. She explains the information back accurately, so she understands it. C. The problem arises before she can weigh anything, because she loses the information. D. Nothing suggests she cannot express a choice. E. The presumption of capacity is a principle of the Act, not one of the functional abilities.
pearl: Delirium often fluctuates, so capacity should be reassessed at a better time of day and information given in short, repeated, written forms to aid retention.
thinking: Explains information accurately ↓ Understanding intact ↓ Forgets within minutes ↓ Cannot keep it long enough to decide ↓ Retention impaired
exam_trap: C, Using or weighing — failing to reach a decision looks like a weighing problem, but she cannot weigh information she has already forgotten.
takeaway: Being unable to retain information long enough to make a decision means failing the retention part of the capacity test.
notes: Checker: Format only: source added. Overlap noted: live BX012 lists the four functional abilities; this item applies them (identify retention failure) - kept.

presentation: Functional test of capacity: using or weighing
stem:
A 47-year-old man with a frontal brain injury is offered a hernia repair. He accurately repeats the procedure and its risks the next day, but when asked to decide he cannot balance any benefit against any risk and changes his answer at random each time he is asked.

Which component of capacity is impaired?
correct_answer: B. Using or weighing the information
why_correct: He understands and remembers the information, but he cannot use it to compare benefits against risks in reaching a decision. This is an impairment of the ability to use or weigh information, one of the four functional abilities under the Mental Capacity Act 2005. Frontal lobe injury can affect this ability while leaving memory and language intact. Source: Mental Capacity Act 2005 section 3, UK Parliament, 2005; Decision-making and mental capacity (NG108), NICE, 2018.
why_wrong: A. He explains the procedure accurately, so understanding is intact. C. He recalls the details the next day, so retention is intact. D. He can state an answer; the problem is how he reaches it. E. The presumption of capacity is a starting principle, not one of the functional abilities.
pearl: People with frontal injury can pass a memory test and talk fluently yet still lack capacity because they cannot weigh information.
thinking: Understands the operation ↓ Remembers it the next day ↓ Cannot balance benefit against risk ↓ Random, shifting answers ↓ Using or weighing impaired
exam_trap: D, Communicating a decision — his answer keeps changing, which looks like a communication problem, but he speaks clearly; the inconsistency comes from being unable to weigh the information.
takeaway: A person who understands and remembers information but cannot balance it to reach a decision fails the using or weighing part of the test.
notes: Checker: Key was longest (option A lengthened). 'Frontal injury commonly affects' softened to 'can affect'. Source added. Overlap with live BX012 noted as for PAN6080.

stem:
A 64-year-old woman with motor neurone disease has lost the ability to speak but uses an eye-gaze communication board. The respiratory team need her decision about starting non-invasive ventilation. She appears to follow the explanation closely and nods appropriately.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: She lacks capacity because she cannot speak
options.B: Her husband should decide on her behalf
options.C: She may have capacity if she can indicate her choice with the board
options.D: An independent mental capacity advocate should make the decision for her
options.E: The team should decide what is in her best interests because she cannot speak

correct_answer: C. She may have capacity if she can indicate her choice with the board
why_correct: Communicating a decision can be done by any means, including writing, signing, gestures or communication aids. The Mental Capacity Act requires all practicable steps to be taken to help a person decide before concluding incapacity. If she can understand, retain and weigh the information and indicate her choice through her eye-gaze board, she has capacity. Source: Mental Capacity Act 2005 sections 1 and 3, UK Parliament, 2005.
why_wrong: A. Loss of speech does not mean loss of capacity if she can communicate another way. B. A spouse has no authority to decide for an adult who has capacity, unless appointed under a relevant lasting power of attorney and she lacks capacity. D. An advocate represents and supports a person but never makes the decision. E. Best-interests decisions apply only if she is shown to lack capacity.
pearl: Speech and language therapists can help assess and support communication in people with speech loss before a capacity judgement is made.
thinking: Cannot speak ↓ Uses an eye-gaze board ↓ Appears to understand ↓ Communication can be by any means ↓ Take all practicable steps ↓ May have capacity
exam_trap: E, Best-interests decision — loss of speech in a serious illness makes the team want to decide for her, but best interests applies only after incapacity is shown, and she may be able to decide.
takeaway: Inability to speak does not mean inability to communicate a decision; support other forms of communication.
notes: Checker: Key was longest (shortened; D and E lengthened). Source added. Overlap noted: u74-g03 PAN10477 (dysphasic stroke patient, wife wants to decide) tests the presumption of capacity rather than communication by any means - kept, but clinician may judge them too close.

stem:
Six months ago a hospital doctor recorded that a 79-year-old man with vascular dementia lacked capacity to manage his finances. He is now on a surgical ward and needs a decision about an elective hernia repair. The ward nurse suggests the earlier assessment can simply be applied.

Which statement best reflects the law on mental capacity?

options.A: The earlier finding of incapacity applies to all later decisions
options.B: Capacity must be assessed for the hernia decision when it needs to be made
options.C: His wife becomes the decision-maker now that dementia is established
options.D: A diagnosis of vascular dementia means he cannot consent to surgery
options.E: A cognitive test score below a set threshold would confirm that he lacks capacity

correct_answer: B. Capacity must be assessed for the hernia decision when it needs to be made
why_correct: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 treats capacity as specific to each decision and to the time it is made. Lacking capacity for complex finances does not mean he lacks capacity to decide about a hernia repair now, so a fresh assessment for this decision is required. Source: Mental Capacity Act 2005 sections 2 and 3, UK Parliament, 2005; Decision-making and mental capacity (NG108), NICE, 2018.
why_wrong: A. An earlier assessment for a different decision cannot be transferred, and capacity can change over time. C. A spouse has no authority to decide unless appointed under a relevant lasting power of attorney. D. A diagnosis never by itself establishes incapacity. E. No test score defines capacity; the functional test does.
pearl: Every adult is presumed to have capacity, and all practicable steps to help the person decide must be taken before concluding otherwise.
thinking: Previous assessment was for finances ↓ New decision is about surgery ↓ Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific ↓ Diagnosis and old findings do not transfer ↓ Reassess for this decision now
exam_trap: A, Relying on the earlier finding — it seems efficient and documented, but capacity for one decision at one time says nothing reliable about a different decision later.
takeaway: Assess capacity afresh for each decision, at the time it needs to be made.
notes: Checker: Key was longest (shortened; E lengthened). Patient name removed from stem (vignettes must be name-free). Source added. Kept in preference to PAN2776 (same learning point).

stem:
A GP registrar in a busy practice asks the practice healthcare assistant to perform phlebotomy and an ECG on a patient with suspected angina, so that the registrar can see other patients.

What is the registrar still responsible for?

options.A: Staying present for the whole of each task
options.B: Making sure the assistant has a doctor's qualifications
options.C: Getting the patient's written consent to the tasks being delegated
options.D: Nothing further, as accountability passes fully to the assistant
options.E: Being satisfied that the assistant is competent for these tasks

correct_answer: E. Being satisfied that the assistant is competent for these tasks
why_correct: When you delegate, you remain responsible for the decision to delegate. The registrar must be satisfied that the assistant has the knowledge, skills and experience for these tasks or will be adequately supervised, give clear instructions, and make sure the results come back for review. Source: Good medical practice, GMC, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Continuous supervision is not needed when the person is competent for the task. B. The person needs competence for the specific task, not the same qualifications. C. Separate written consent to delegation is not required. D. The doctor remains responsible for the overall care and for the decision to delegate.
pearl: Delegation and referral differ: in referral, responsibility for the patient's care is transferred in part or in full, whereas in delegation the doctor keeps responsibility for the overall management.
thinking: Task handed to another professional ↓ This is delegation, not referral ↓ Doctor keeps responsibility for the decision to delegate ↓ Must check competence and give clear instructions ↓ Ensure competence
exam_trap: D, Accountability passes to the assistant — it seems logical that the person doing the task owns it, but the doctor stays responsible for choosing to delegate and for the patient's overall care.
takeaway: When delegating, make sure the person is competent for the task; you remain responsible for that decision.
notes: Checker: Key was longest (tightened). Source added: the separate GMC 'Delegation and referral' guidance (2013-2024) is superseded; Good medical practice 2024 now carries the delegation standard.

stem:
A first-year foundation doctor covering the respiratory ward is asked to review a 71-year-old man with known COPD whose oxygen saturation keeps dropping despite nebulisers and steroids. A blood gas shows worsening hypercapnic acidosis and the doctor recognises he may need non-invasive ventilation, which the doctor has never set up or prescribed.

What should the doctor do?

options.A: Leave the plan for the consultant ward round
options.B: Set up non-invasive ventilation alone using an online guide
options.C: Increase the oxygen to high flow and reassess later
options.D: Contact the medical registrar promptly for senior help
options.E: Repeat the nebulisers and recheck the blood gas tomorrow

correct_answer: D. Contact the medical registrar promptly for senior help
why_correct: The doctor has recognised the likely problem but the next step is beyond their competence. Doctors must recognise and work within the limits of their competence and seek help when needed, so prompt escalation to the medical registrar is right, as this man is deteriorating and needs an urgent decision about ventilatory support. Source: Good medical practice, GMC, 2024; NIV in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure guideline, BTS/ICS, 2016.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for the ward round delays treatment in a patient getting worse. B. Starting a treatment you are not trained to give puts the patient at risk. C. High-flow oxygen may worsen hypercapnia in COPD and does not secure senior help. E. Deferring reassessment to the next day is unsafe in worsening acidosis.
pearl: In COPD patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, oxygen is titrated to a target saturation of 88 to 92 percent.
thinking: Patient deteriorating despite initial treatment ↓ Doctor recognises likely need for NIV ↓ Task is beyond the doctor's competence ↓ Delay is unsafe ↓ Seek senior help promptly
exam_trap: B, Setting it up alone — it seems proactive, but acting beyond your competence without supervision can harm the patient.
takeaway: Recognise the limits of your competence and seek senior help promptly for a deteriorating patient.
notes: Checker: Format only: source added. Overlap noted: u74-g06 PAN1368 (out of depth with a deteriorating post-op patient -> call senior help) and PAN1638 (untrained procedure -> ask supervision) share the 'limits of competence' point in different scenarios - kept, clinician to confirm.

presentation: Persistent escalation when concerns are not acted on
stem:
A foundation doctor on a surgical ward bleeps the on-call registrar about a 54-year-old man with suspected anastomotic leak who is becoming more tachycardic and hypotensive. The registrar, busy in theatre, says they will come when they can. An hour later the patient is worse and still has not been seen.

What should the foundation doctor do next?

options.A: Escalate further, for example to the on-call consultant or outreach team
options.B: Move the patient to another ward where a different team might be able to see him
options.C: Record the earlier call in the notes and keep waiting
options.D: Carry on hourly observations until the registrar arrives
options.E: Ask the morning consultant ward round to review him

correct_answer: A. Escalate further, for example to the on-call consultant or outreach team
why_correct: If a deteriorating patient is not being reviewed, the doctor must keep escalating through the hierarchy until appropriate help arrives, for example to the consultant or the critical care outreach team, and should document each step. Patient safety comes before concern about bypassing a busy senior. Source: Good medical practice, GMC, 2024; National Early Warning Score 2, Royal College of Physicians, 2017.
why_wrong: B. Moving him does not secure senior review and may delay it. C. Documentation without further action leaves him at risk. D. Observations alone do not bring the review he needs. E. Waiting until morning could allow avoidable harm.
pearl: Most hospitals have a critical care outreach or rapid response team that can be called directly for a deteriorating patient, whatever the grade of the caller.
thinking: Deteriorating patient escalated once ↓ Senior unavailable and patient worse ↓ Initial escalation has failed ↓ Duty to persist ↓ Escalate higher and document
exam_trap: C, Documenting and waiting — it creates a record that you raised the concern, but it leaves the patient unreviewed while getting worse.
takeaway: If the first escalation does not produce a review, keep escalating until help arrives.
notes: Checker: Key was longest (shortened; B lengthened). Source added. Kept in preference to PAN1277 (same learning point).

stem:
A man in his forties has been kept waiting at his GP surgery well beyond his appointment time. When he is finally called in, he speaks loudly and complains that nobody told him about the delay, but he is not threatening and makes no aggressive gestures.

What is the most appropriate way for the GP to respond?

options.A: Tell him the delay was caused by other patients and is not the GP's fault
options.B: Call the police to report disruptive behaviour
options.C: Ask the practice manager to remove him from the premises
options.D: Match his volume so that he stops interrupting
options.E: Stay calm, listen and acknowledge his frustration about the wait

correct_answer: E. Stay calm, listen and acknowledge his frustration about the wait
why_correct: He is frustrated but not threatening. A calm tone, active listening and acknowledging his concern, often with an apology for the wait, are the most effective ways to de-escalate and allow the consultation to continue. Source: Violence and aggression: short-term management in mental health, health and community settings (NG10), NICE, 2015.
why_wrong: A. Deflecting blame dismisses his concern and may inflame things. B. Police involvement is disproportionate when there is no threat. C. Removing him is disproportionate for verbal frustration. D. Raising your own voice is likely to escalate the situation.
pearl: If anger does escalate to threats or violence, the priority becomes personal and staff safety: leave the room, use the alarm and seek help.
thinking: Patient angry about a delay ↓ No threat or violence ↓ Aim is to de-escalate ↓ Calm tone, listen, acknowledge ↓ Continue the consultation
exam_trap: A, Explaining that it is not the GP's fault — it may be true, but it sounds defensive and ignores what he is feeling.
takeaway: Calm listening and acknowledgement defuse most verbal anger.

stem:
A GP registrar is seeing a 47-year-old man with a new diagnosis of hypertension who also has type 2 diabetes and early kidney disease. She realises she is not sure which antihypertensive is currently recommended first for someone with his combination of conditions.

What is the most appropriate way to decide on treatment?

options.A: Check current national guidance, such as NICE, and apply it to his circumstances
options.B: Prescribe the medicine he would prefer even if there are safety concerns
options.C: Rely on an old textbook from the practice library without checking for newer advice
options.D: Follow the guideline rigidly without considering his other conditions
options.E: Make the decision alone without asking colleagues

correct_answer: A. Check current national guidance, such as NICE, and apply it to his circumstances
why_correct: Good practice is to base decisions on current, relevant evidence-based guidance while applying clinical judgement to the individual patient, including comorbidities, preferences and interactions. When unsure, doctors should also feel free to ask senior colleagues. This keeps care safe, up to date and personalised. Source: Good medical practice, GMC, 2024; Hypertension in adults (NG136), NICE, 2019.
why_wrong: B. Patient preference matters but cannot override safety. C. Outdated sources may give recommendations that have since changed. D. Guidelines support but do not replace judgement for individual patients. E. Seeking advice when uncertain is expected and promotes safe care.
pearl: The GMC expects doctors to recognise and work within the limits of their competence and to keep their knowledge up to date.
thinking: Doctor uncertain about best management ↓ Current guidance gives the evidence base ↓ Patient has several conditions ↓ Apply guidance with judgement ↓ Ask colleagues if still unsure
exam_trap: D, Following the guideline rigidly — it seems the safest evidence-based option, but guidelines must be adapted to the individual, especially with comorbidities.
takeaway: Use current evidence-based guidance together with clinical judgement, and ask colleagues when unsure.
notes: Checker: Key was longest (shortened; C lengthened). Source added.

presentation: Communicating the limitations of a negative test
stem:
A 62-year-old man returns a home faecal immunochemical test through the bowel cancer screening programme and receives a normal result. He has no bowel symptoms. At a GP appointment for another problem, he asks whether this means he definitely cannot have bowel cancer.

What is the best response?

options.A: Explain it lowers but does not exclude the risk of cancer, and say which symptoms to report
options.B: Reassure him that bowel cancer has now been ruled out by the normal screening test
options.C: Arrange a colonoscopy so the normal result can be confirmed before discussing it further
options.D: Tell him the result is normal and that he will not need to take part in any further screening
options.E: Advise him to contact the screening hub, as they are the only ones who can answer this

correct_answer: A. Explain it lowers but does not exclude the risk of cancer, and say which symptoms to report
why_correct: No screening test is perfect, and a normal faecal immunochemical test lowers the probability of bowel cancer without excluding it. Honest explanation of this uncertainty, together with clear safety-netting about rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, weight loss or other symptoms, lets him make informed decisions and seek help early. He will also be invited again in the next screening round. Source: Bowel cancer screening programme overview, GOV.UK (NHS screening programmes), 2026; Decision making and consent, GMC, 2020.
why_wrong: B. False reassurance may delay presentation if symptoms develop. C. Colonoscopy is not indicated for an asymptomatic man with a normal result. D. Screening is repeated at regular intervals, so this is incorrect. E. He has asked his own doctor a reasonable question that can be answered now.
pearl: Safety-netting should state which symptoms to look out for, how soon to act and where to seek help.
thinking: Asymptomatic, normal screening result ↓ Asks if cancer is definitely excluded ↓ No test has perfect sensitivity ↓ Be honest about limitations ↓ Safety-net with specific symptoms
exam_trap: B, Saying cancer has been ruled out — it is comforting and matches a normal result, but it overstates the test and can delay presentation later.
takeaway: Be honest about what a test can and cannot exclude, and safety-net clearly.
notes: Checker: Key was much longest (shortened; B-E lengthened). 'Much less likely' softened to 'lowers' (a normal screening FIT lowers but does not remove risk). Source added; screening age band and 2-yearly recall checked (50-74, England).

stem:
A 57-year-old woman is seen on the gastroenterology ward after a CT scan for painless jaundice. The report describes a mass in the head of the pancreas that is suspicious for malignancy, and an endoscopic biopsy has been booked. She asks the registrar, 'Does this mean I have cancer?'

What is the best way to respond?

options.A: Tell her the mass is most likely a harmless cyst
options.B: Tell her it is cancer so she can begin preparing herself
options.C: Decline to discuss what the scan shows until the biopsy result is available
options.D: Say the scan shows a worrying mass, cancer is possible but not confirmed, and explain next steps
options.E: Tell her the oncologist will explain everything at a later appointment once all the results are back

correct_answer: D. Say the scan shows a worrying mass, cancer is possible but not confirmed, and explain next steps
why_correct: She has asked a direct question and is entitled to an honest answer at a pace that suits her. The registrar should explain what the scan shows, that cancer is a real possibility but the biopsy is needed to confirm it, and what will happen next and when. This avoids both false reassurance and a premature diagnosis, and allows her to ask questions and involve family. Source: Decision making and consent, GMC, 2020.
why_wrong: A. False reassurance is dishonest and undermines trust when results return. B. Stating a diagnosis before it is confirmed may be wrong and causes avoidable distress. C. Refusing to discuss known findings leaves her anxious and uninformed. E. Deferring to another clinician avoids a reasonable question the team can answer now.
pearl: Checking what the patient already knows and how much they want to hear before giving information helps tailor difficult conversations.
thinking: Imaging suspicious but not diagnostic ↓ Patient asks directly ↓ Avoid false reassurance and premature diagnosis ↓ Explain known, uncertain and next steps ↓ Offer support and follow-up
exam_trap: C, Waiting for the biopsy — holding back can seem kind, but she already knows something is wrong and silence increases anxiety and erodes trust.
takeaway: When a diagnosis is uncertain, explain what is known, what is not, and what happens next.
notes: Checker: Stem lacked the blank line before the question (fixed). Key was much longest (shortened; C and E lengthened). Source added.

stem:
A 4-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her father because she has been crying when her nappy is changed and is not moving her left leg. He cannot recall any fall or injury. A radiograph shows a corner fracture at the distal femoral metaphysis.

What is the significance of this finding?

options.A: It strongly suggests non-accidental injury and needs a safeguarding response
options.B: It is a typical accidental injury from routine handling such as nappy changes at this age
options.D: Osteogenesis imperfecta is the most likely cause
options.E: It makes abuse unlikely because there is no bruising

correct_answer: A. It strongly suggests non-accidental injury and needs a safeguarding response
why_correct: Metaphyseal corner or bucket-handle fractures, the classic metaphyseal lesion, result from forceful twisting or shaking of a limb and are strongly associated with abuse in infants. She is non-mobile and there is no explanation, which adds to the concern. The paediatric team and children's social care should be involved and a skeletal survey and further assessment arranged in line with safeguarding procedures. Source: Child maltreatment: when to suspect maltreatment in under 18s (CG89), NICE, 2009 (updated 2017); Child Protection Evidence: fractures, RCPCH, 2020.
why_wrong: B. A non-mobile infant rarely sustains accidental long-bone fractures, and normal handling does not produce this pattern. C. Rickets can cause metaphyseal changes but is an uncommon explanation and does not remove the duty to act on safeguarding concerns. D. Osteogenesis imperfecta is rare and still requires investigation alongside safeguarding. E. Bruising is often absent in abusive fractures.
pearl: Any fracture in a non-mobile infant without a clear, consistent explanation should prompt safeguarding assessment.
thinking: Infant, not yet mobile ↓ No history of trauma ↓ Classic metaphyseal lesion on radiograph ↓ Strongly associated with abuse ↓ Safeguarding referral and skeletal survey
exam_trap: D, Osteogenesis imperfecta — bone fragility is a recognised differential, but it is rare and does not explain away the need for a safeguarding response.
takeaway: Metaphyseal fractures in infants are highly suggestive of non-accidental injury and need safeguarding action.
notes: Checker: Key was longest (shortened; B reworded/lengthened as a plausible 'handling' distractor, why_wrong B updated). Source added. Overlap noted: live PED046/BX965, parked PAQ966 and u74-g05 PAQ11601 teach 'unexplained fracture in a non-mobile infant -> safeguarding'; this item's distinct point is that the classic metaphyseal lesion itself is strongly associated with abuse - kept, clinician to confirm it is distinct enough.

stem:
A practice nurse in a GP surgery has just given a 70-year-old man his intramuscular vaccine. The sharps bin is on a trolley beside her, and she reaches for the needle cap out of habit.

What is the correct action?

options.A: Do not recap; put the needle and syringe straight into the sharps bin
options.B: Resheathe the needle carefully using both hands, then put it in the sharps bin
options.C: Bend the needle over first so that it cannot be reused by anyone
options.D: Place the uncapped needle and syringe in the clinical waste bag
options.E: Leave it on the tray and clear everything up after the next patient

correct_answer: A. Do not recap; put the needle and syringe straight into the sharps bin
why_correct: Resheathing used needles is a common cause of needlestick injury. Used sharps should be disposed of immediately by the person who used them, into a sharps container at the point of use, without recapping, bending or breaking the needle. This reduces the risk of blood-borne virus transmission to staff. Source: Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013, regulation 5, UK Government, 2013; National infection prevention and control manual for England, NHS England, current edition (accessed 2026).
why_wrong: B. Two-handed recapping is a well-known cause of needlestick injuries. C. Bending or breaking needles increases injury risk. D. Waste bags can be pierced, endangering staff who handle them. E. Leaving sharps lying around exposes others to injury.
pearl: After a needlestick injury, encourage the wound to bleed, wash it with soap and running water, and report it promptly so the need for post-exposure prophylaxis can be assessed.
thinking: Used needle after injection ↓ Recapping causes needlestick injuries ↓ Sharps bin at point of use ↓ User disposes of their own sharps immediately ↓ Do not recap, bend or leave lying
exam_trap: B, Careful two-handed resheathing — it feels tidy and safe, but recapping is exactly how many needlestick injuries happen.
takeaway: Never recap used needles; dispose of them immediately into a sharps container at the point of use.
notes: Checker: Reinstated: partner g05 PAN1524 dropped. Full recheck: no live or held item tests recapping/disposal at point of use (live BX016/BX563/BX490/ID024 cover first aid and PEP after a sharps injury, a different learning point); no kept item repeats it. Clinical content verified: the Sharps Regulations 2013 reg 5(1)(c) bar capping used needles unless risk-assessed with a suitable device, and require secure sharps containers close to where sharps are used. Key was much longest (shortened; B lengthened, C-E reworded slightly). Source line and sources added.

stem:
On a surgical ward, an FY1 doctor adjusts the infusion pump settings and moves the bedside table out of the way. She then turns to palpate the abdomen of a 68-year-old man who had a bowel resection two days ago.

Which step is most important at this point to protect the patient from infection?

options.A: Put on a pair of non-sterile gloves straight away
options.B: Clean her hands thoroughly once the abdominal examination is finished
options.C: Wipe down the infusion pump with a detergent wipe
options.D: Wash her hands at the sink when the ward round ends
options.E: Decontaminate her hands with alcohol rub before touching him

correct_answer: E. Decontaminate her hands with alcohol rub before touching him
why_correct: Touching the pump and furniture will have contaminated her hands with organisms from the patient environment. Cleaning hands immediately before touching the patient is the first of the WHO five moments for hand hygiene and stops those organisms reaching a vulnerable post-operative patient. Alcohol hand rub is suitable as her hands are not visibly soiled. Source: National infection prevention and control manual for England, NHS England, current edition (accessed 2026).
why_wrong: A. Gloves put on over contaminated hands still carry organisms and do not replace hand hygiene. B. Hand hygiene afterwards protects others, not this patient from what is already on her hands. C. Cleaning equipment does nothing for the organisms already on her hands. D. Hands must be cleaned at each patient contact, not deferred to the end of the round.
pearl: Alcohol hand rub is adequate for most moments, but soap and water are needed when hands are visibly soiled or when caring for patients with diarrhoea such as suspected Clostridioides difficile, because alcohol does not kill spores.
thinking: Hands touched equipment and the bed space ↓ Environment carries organisms ↓ About to touch the patient ↓ WHO moment one: before patient contact ↓ Clean hands now, before examining
exam_trap: A, Putting on gloves — it feels protective, but gloves pulled on over contaminated hands transfer organisms to the patient and never replace hand hygiene.
takeaway: Clean your hands immediately before touching a patient, even when you are about to put on gloves.

stem:
A healthcare assistant in a care home tells the visiting doctor that she does not bother cleaning her hands between residents because she always wears gloves when helping them wash.

Which statement should the doctor use to correct her?

options.A: Gloves give complete protection, so her current practice is acceptable
options.B: Gloves can be kept on between residents provided they are not torn
options.C: Hand hygiene is needed only before aseptic procedures, not personal care
options.D: Double gloving would remove the need for hand hygiene
options.E: Hands must be cleaned before gloves go on and after they come off

correct_answer: E. Hands must be cleaned before gloves go on and after they come off
why_correct: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene. They can have tiny perforations, and hands are commonly contaminated when gloves are removed. Hands must therefore be cleaned before gloves are put on and after they are taken off, and gloves must be changed between residents and tasks. Source: National infection prevention and control manual for England, NHS England, current edition (accessed 2026).
why_wrong: A. Gloves reduce but do not eliminate contamination of the hands. B. Gloves are single use and must be changed between residents. C. Hand hygiene applies to all patient contact, including personal care. D. Extra gloves still leave hands contaminated on removal.
pearl: Gloves should be worn only when there is a risk of contact with blood, body fluids, mucous membranes or non-intact skin; unnecessary glove use increases cross-infection and skin damage.
thinking: Carer relies on gloves alone ↓ Gloves can leak and hands are contaminated on removal ↓ Gloves are single use per resident and task ↓ Hand hygiene before and after gloves ↓ Correct her practice
exam_trap: B, Keeping intact gloves on between residents — it sounds economical, but gloves carry organisms from one person to the next and must be changed and hands cleaned each time.
takeaway: Gloves never replace hand hygiene; clean hands before putting them on and after taking them off.
notes: Checker: Key was longest (tightened). Source added; NIPCM: 'Always perform hand hygiene before putting on and after removing gloves'. Kept as the single hand-hygiene-and-gloves item from this batch (PAN4857 and PAN1567 dropped as repeats).
